What's new in Vekrun 0.7.5

Vekrun now understands many more kinds of projects. For each one it knows how to find it in an existing repository, set it up in the build machine, build it, run its tests, and prove the result. Each kind of project is described by a "recipe". This release adds more than 70 of them. Next to each group below we say how far it has been proven:

- **Proven end to end**: a real project, or one made from the official starter, was set up, built and tested by Vekrun in a build machine. Most also have a deliberately broken copy that failed where it should.
- **Partly proven**: some of it ran in a build machine (for example setup and tests on one real project), or it reuses a setup proven for a close relative, but it didn't get the full set of checks on its own.
- **Known, not yet proven**: Vekrun recognises it and has the setup, but no build machine has run it yet. It is used only when you ask for it, never picked by itself.

JavaScript and TypeScript apps
• React (Vite), Vue, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Angular, AngularJS, NestJS and Express: proven end to end. Vekrun builds the app, runs its tests, starts it, and checks the page in a real browser inside the build machine. Older AngularJS projects get their old Node version (for example Node 10) from the project's own CI settings.
• A plain Node.js service uses the same setup as the apps above (partly proven: no separate run of its own).
• Browser tests: Playwright, Cypress and Karma are found from the project's own files. Vekrun installs the browser they need and runs them: proven end to end. Karma gets a headless Chromium.
• Docker Compose services and Dev Containers in a repository are now recipes of their own. A Dev Container's Node version, environment and setup command are respected: proven end to end.
• Tailwind CSS v4 now also works on React and Vue apps built with Vite, and on Nuxt; shadcn/ui on React with Vite: proven end to end. Tailwind on SvelteKit and Angular, and Tailwind v3 on these apps, are partly proven. Asking for shadcn/ui on a Vue or Nuxt app now says plainly that it needs React.

Languages, runtimes and packages
• Go (modules, and older GOPATH projects, linked into their workspace for you), Rust applications and Rust libraries, Elixir, Python packages, npm packages and Ruby gems: proven end to end. For a library, Vekrun also checks that it would package correctly (a dry run: nothing is ever published).
• Erlang/OTP and Elixir come from hex.pm's official builds, and each download is checked against its published checksum.
• Old PHP (7.x, 8.0) that the system no longer packages is set up from the official PHP image (partly proven: setup ran in a build machine, the tests were run by hand).
• Java with Maven and Spring Boot: partly proven (Spring PetClinic set up, built and its 79 tests passed).
• Plain Ruby projects use the Ruby setup proven for gems (partly proven).
• Java with Gradle, ASP.NET Core and .NET, Phoenix, plain PHP and Symfony: known, not yet proven. ASP.NET Core's setup works, but a real project crashed in the build machine on this Mac's chip, so it is not claimed yet.
• .NET Framework projects (Windows only) are recognised and explained: Vekrun says why it can't build them here instead of trying.

Databases and services
• PostgreSQL (and PostgreSQL 16 as a fixed version), MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, MongoDB, Redis and Valkey: proven end to end. Each one is set up for the project's tests and then checked: a real write and read, and a wrong password must be refused.
• PostgreSQL 14, 15 and 17 as fixed versions use the route PostgreSQL 16 proved (partly proven).
• PostgreSQL extensions: pgvector, PostGIS, pg_partman, TimescaleDB and btree_gist. Each is installed and then used once by a real query: proven end to end.
• Prisma: proven end to end. It gets a database of its own in the build machine, so it can never drop your app's tables. Drizzle: known, not yet proven.
• Local email (Mailpit), S3-compatible storage, Meilisearch search, a local sign-in provider (OIDC), and background workers (Sidekiq, Celery, BullMQ): proven end to end. Every service listens only inside the build machine, and its downloads are pinned and checksum-checked.
• Image and video tools (libvips, ImageMagick, ffmpeg): proven end to end.
• OpenSearch and Elasticsearch: known, not yet proven (they need more memory than the shared test machine had).

Mobile and desktop apps (built on your Mac, never in the build machine)
• Flutter for iOS and Android, Expo, native SwiftUI iOS apps, Kotlin Android apps, Tauri and Electron: proven end to end. Vekrun builds the app with your Mac's own tools, runs its tests, launches it on a fresh simulator, emulator or as a real window, and takes a screenshot of that window only. A desktop app that crashes while loading is now caught.
• Flutter for macOS: partly proven (tests and build ran, the app wasn't launched). React Native without Expo: partly proven (its setup wasn't run live).
• Ignite and watchOS apps: known, not yet proven. watchOS couldn't be built here because the watchOS platform isn't installed in this Mac's Xcode.

Sites, backends and automation tools
• WordPress themes and plugins (with WooCommerce), Ghost, PocketBase, n8n and Node-RED: proven end to end. Vekrun runs a pinned version of each in the build machine, reachable only from inside it. It loads your theme, migrations, flows or workflows, checks pages and APIs (including that an anonymous visitor is refused where they should be), and takes a browser screenshot. Supabase and Firebase projects are now first-class recipes too, proven end to end against their local emulators.
• Strapi and Zapier apps: partly proven (one real project each was built and tested).
• Drupal, Joomla, Magento, BigCommerce, Payload, Sanity, Appwrite, Convex, Xano, Backendless, Windmill and Make: Vekrun recognises them and explains in plain words what it can and can't do for them. It doesn't set them up.
• Where your project deploys (Render, Vercel, Netlify, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, Cloudflare, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner): Vekrun reads the deploy settings file, says whether it looks right (for example "fly.toml is missing app"), and records it with the proof. It never deploys and never contacts the provider.

Extensions, plugins, libraries and SDKs
• Chrome (Manifest V3) extensions, WXT, Firefox extensions, VS Code extensions, TypeScript libraries that ship both ESM and CommonJS, and OpenAPI clients made with openapi-typescript: proven end to end. A browser extension is validated and actually loaded in a headless Chromium. Its background worker has to start and its popup has to render. A VS Code extension is packaged into a local .vsix and its tests run inside a real VS Code. Nothing is ever published, signed or uploaded to a store.
• Swift packages, CMake and Meson (C and C++), Zig and Deno projects: proven end to end, including real projects such as swift-argument-parser (517 tests) and cJSON. Bun projects too, when you ask for Bun. A Node project that only happens to have a bun.lock keeps its Node setup.
• Obsidian plugins: partly proven (built and checked; running one needs the Obsidian app).
• Plasmo, Figma plugins, JetBrains plugins, OpenAPI Generator and Kotlin JVM libraries: known, not yet proven.

How Vekrun picks recipes
• For an existing project, Vekrun picks recipes from the project's own files, using one rule for all of them. Browser test runners, Docker Compose, Dev Containers, Stripe, Tailwind, pgvector, Prisma and the like attach to what was found. A Rust, Java, Go or Elixir project now gets its own build check. Vekrun never overrides the framework it detected, and recipes that aren't proven yet are only used when you ask for them.
• If one found recipe can't be combined with the project, only that one is left out, with a short note saying why. The others are kept.
• A language that Vekrun sets up itself is installed once, at the version your project pins.
• Rust's installer is now pinned to a release and checked against its checksum before it runs.
